Uniform Title: *Ṣaṭtriṃśattattvasandoha* Main Title: *Ṣaṭtriṃśattattvasandoha* with the Commentary (*vṛtti*) of Rājānakānanda Commentator: Rājānakānanda
Editor: Śāstrī M R Description: E-text transcribed from volume 13 of the Kashmir Series of Texts and Studies.
Notes: This e-text was transcribed by the staff of Muktabodha under the supervision of Mark S.G. Dyczkowski. Revision 0: March 19, 2005.
Publisher: Research Department, Jammu and Kashmir State Publication Year: 1918 Publication City: Srinagar
Country of publication: India.
This supreme form, by its own will, [desires] to create this entire world.
That first vibration which throbbed is called the Śiva-tattva by those who know it. || 1 ||

For here, in this non-dualistic system of independent Śiva, the Supreme Lord is autonomous, his essential nature being dense consciousness; by means of His own power called "autonomy," He eternally manifests as the various worlds, elements, and principles, beginning with Śiva and ending with the Earth.
Because his nature consists of play and so forth, he performs the fivefold cosmic act; although in reality there is no succession,
in the creation of the universe he manifests even succession through a transcendental relation of cause and effect, which is essentially nothing more than a mere appearance.
Even though it is inexpressible, by its own will alone, it manifests upon the wall of its own self the designations of the various principles (tattvas) beginning with Śiva;
and even while being so, it does so through the reflective awareness of the nature of Kula, which consists of the thirty-six principles.

A certain great Mahāmaheśvara, graced by the descent of the Supreme Lord’s power (parameśa-śaktipāta), [speaks] in order to awaken the understanding of the true intention: that one does not abandon the state which is undivided, which fills the universe, whose essence is the reflective awareness of one's own creative wonder (svacamatkāra-vimarśa), and which is a mass of unsurpassed bliss (anuttarānanda).
He composed the *Tattvakramaprakriyā* in twenty-one Āryā verses,
beginning with the words "yadayam" and so forth, concerning the supreme form of the Blessed Lord Parameśvara.
The first state of the desire to emit the universe— which exists as one with His own self, which is a mass of light—
is the initial impulse of manifestation within Himself, like a city in a mirror;
it is designated as the *Śivatattva* because of its sovereignty and its being filled with the five powers.

On the pure path (śuddhādhvan), the manifestation of the creation of the principles (tattva-sṛṣṭi) occurs in succession, with consciousness (cit) and the other [principles] as predominant, [proceeding] from the Supreme Śiva, who is a dense mass of the light of consciousness, through Māyā, Vidyā, and so forth.
Because it is not undermined by conceptual alternatives such as difference or non-difference, absolute sovereignty alone is preeminent in the creation and dissolution of the universe;
for it embraces all those infinite collections of powers, even as will be explained hereafter.
Because He possesses freedom in assuming various forms, there is no loss of His primordial nature;
that very will, being pure and eternally inherent, is Power (śakti).
The seed of the entire world, both moving and unmoving, which is withdrawn within himself. || 2 ||

(p. 3) His own power of independent will (*svatantrēcchā-śakti*), which is non-different from him, becomes the *śakti-tattva*—the state of being the seed—as the universe yet to arise remains latent within him; and although this power is an attribute of the possessor of power (*śāktimat*), it is not separate from him in the manner asserted by other philosophical systems.

In this state of *naiṣkarmya* (freedom from action), because of the purity of desire, it is designated by various names such as "the heart," "self-reflection" (*vimarśa*), "essence," "wave," and so forth, in those respective philosophical systems.
For it is the Supreme Lord himself who, through the surging of His own sovereignty, [manifests in these forms].

By means of the gradations of the wonder of full self-identity (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*), one presides over the state of power (*śaktidaśā*); herein, the predominance belongs to the power of bliss (*ānandaśakti*). || 2 ||
Having completely enveloped the universe— which has been projected by His own power of will— as His very self,
He alone dwells as the entirety [of existence].
Sadāśiva is said to be ever devoted to bestowing grace. || 3 ||

The state of the *sadāśiva-tattva* arises from that very Supreme Lord’s manifestation of the universe— which is projected by His own sovereignty— within Himself alone, by means of its locus in pure consciousness-only, and thus by being designated as "Being" (*sat*). In that state:
Because the "this-aspect" (idamaṃśa) is indistinct due to its being like a painting that has only just been opened,
there is a predominance of will (icchā); therefore, he possesses a relish for the rasa of play characterized by the desire to perfectly manifest externally the entire future mass of entities.
Because one who is devoted to bestowing grace takes up the stage belonging to that [level], it is therefore said that he "dwells" there. || 3 ||
Perceiving the entire universe subsequently as "this," the Lord becomes [manifest];
that is Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*).
The notion of non-difference between "this-ness" (yadanta) and "I-ness" (ahantā). || 4 ||

Thus, because the universe manifests sequentially, when it is clearly perceived as having pure consciousness alone as its substratum, it is consecrated within the "I" aspect; consequently, that very Supreme Lord ascends to the state of the *īśvara-tattva*, wherein the entire range of objects of knowledge [is subsumed].
The predominance of the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) arises from the clear manifestation [of objects].

The state of Sadāśiva occurs because of the predominance of the internal dimension, whereas the state of Īśvara occurs due to the predominance of the orientation toward external existence; this is the distinction between these two.

When the "this-ness" aspect (*idantā*), whose differentiation has fully emerged, flashes forth as the "I-ness" aspect (*ahamaṃśa*) according to the analogy of two scales held perfectly level, that is the *śuddhavidyā* principle. Here, because the universe is perceived with extreme clarity, the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) is predominant.
And to this extent, pure sovereignty itself manifests through various diversities;
thus, it is the Pure Path (śuddhādhvan). || 4 ||
The illusion (*māyā*) is the cognition of difference regarding all individual souls (*jīva*), who are born from its own parts; it is eternally and unrestrainedly His [power].
It indeed restrains worldly existence, just as the shore restrains the ocean. || 5 ||
Furthermore, on the impure path, the Supreme Lord himself,
through the play of concealing his own nature, assumes the state of Aghora-Bhaṭṭāraka in the form of a Mantramaheśvara, by virtue of his power to accomplish the impossible.
By means of its power of *māyā*, [the Lord] manifests for the sake of accomplishing the experience (*bhoga*) of the individual souls (*aṇu*)— which are distinct from Himself and from one another—

the entire aggregate of insentient and sentient things, beginning with *kalā* and ending with the earth, both sequentially and non-sequentially; therein, due to the impurity of *māyā* (*māyīyamala*), which consists of the manifestation of difference within those things that are like His own limbs, [the soul perceives them as separate].
Within the class of insentient objects of cognition, it is consciousness itself that, through its differentiation, is called the principle of *māyā*,
by which its unrestrained sovereignty is obstructed, just as the power of the waves of the ocean is checked by the shoreline. || 5 ||
With his form thus limited and all his powers contracted,
this person is like the sun reddened by twilight.
With its power withdrawn, it is incapable even of manifesting itself.

Although that conscious self (cidātman) is immutable, when it undergoes a state of destitution of power following the contraction of its own powers, it receives the name "puruṣa," which is synonymous with "aṇu" (the atom); thus, by having its powers withdrawn, it becomes a limited self.
When one is incapable of recognizing even one's own sovereignty and wanders through various wombs,

yet later— through the varying intensity of the descent of grace (*śaktipāta*)— one recognizes one's own sovereignty as made manifest by *vidyā*, and perceives the universe as being as if it were one's own limb, then one attains the state of a living Śiva (*jīvacchivabhāva*).
He returns to his original state. || 6 ||
He possesses many powers, such as complete agency and so forth;
through contraction, these become contracted.
In this way, they indeed become established in the form of the *kalās* and so forth. || 7 ||

Precisely because the Supreme Lord is never dissociated from His power of absolute freedom (*svātantrya-śakti*), which encompasses all other powers, He possesses manifold powers; yet, through the assumption of limitation (*saṃkoca*), all those powers become contracted and [manifest] as the five categories (*tattva*) beginning with *kalā*.
They attain growth.

These five—omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), omnipotence (*sarvakartṛtā*), contentment (*tṛpti*), permanence (*nityatā*), and sovereignty (*svātantrya*)—are twofold according to the distinction between pure and impure; [the former] pertains to the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*).
It is pure, yet it is impure by virtue of being within the domain of saṃsāra. || 7 ||
That universal agency of his, when contracted, is directed toward only a few objects;
[he is thus] this limited agent.
That which impels is designated by the name "kalā. || 8 ||

Because His true nature is concealed, the power of the Supreme Lord, whose own power is restrained, becomes the power of universal agency; through the act of *kalana*— which consists in the kindling of limited agency within the state of the finite subjects such as the vital breath (*prāṇa*)—
it is cast downward and attains the nature of the *kalā*-tattva, by virtue of which [the subject perceives] only "something" (*kiñcit*).
The atom is not capable of acting everywhere; thus, it does not possess universal agency. || 8 ||
His power of omniscience,
though limited in its physical form and directed only toward a small portion of what is knowable,
produces knowledge.
is called "Vidyā" by the ancient wise ones. || 9 ||
Thus, when the power of that very [consciousness] assumes contraction by producing knowledge directed toward only a limited portion of the knowable, it is the *vidyā-tattva*;
for it is by *vidyā* alone that objects reflected upon the mirror of the intellect (*buddhi*) are discerned.
Because it is impossible to distinguish that [object] due to its being mixed with qualities, therefore, the discernment of the object occurs through knowledge alone. || 9 ||
His power is eternally full and satisfied, yet when it becomes limited, it takes delight in worldly enjoyments.
She has constantly attained the state of the reality-principle of passion. || 10 ||

The power of the Supreme Lord known as eternal and perfectly complete satisfaction (nityaparipūrṇatṛpti), having undergone limitation, becomes the principle of attachment (rāgatattva) through a mere general clinging in the form of the thought, "May something be mine," directed toward whatever is regarded as desirable.

(8) But the attachment to specific objects is, for this very [consciousness], almost like a budding; this alone is the cause, in a certain portion, of the previously mentioned *kalā* and *vidyā*. || 10 ||
That eternity of his, having extracted its power by bestowing both destruction and arising,
acts as the determiner of limitation.
She would be fashioned in the form of the reality of time. || 11 ||
The power called eternity belonging to the conscious self (cidātman), which is not limited by time, assumes a state of subordination and,

through the conceptualization of agency colored by effects, joins the individual soul (aṇu) with time— which consists in the manifestation of a sequence beginning with *tuṭi*— and is thus designated as the principle of Time (*kālatattva*), whereby this soul [becomes bound].
That which is characterized by the sequence of the activities of the elements and so forth falls under the sway of time. || 11 ||
That very power of his called autonomy, when characterized by contraction,
renders him helpless regarding what ought and ought not to be done.
Necessity (niyati) made this final rule certain for him. || 12 ||
(p. 9) It is precisely this sovereignty of the supreme subject that, when contracting,

manifests as the principle of necessity (*niyati*), because by establishing a restriction regarding what is to be done and what is not to be done, it ensures that only a specific cause produces a specific effect, and not something indeterminate.

Enveloped by this sheath of *kalā* and the rest, he experiences a poverty of power; thus, having received only a small portion [of his own glory] through the medium of *kalā* and the other categories, he is called a "bound soul" (*paśu*). || 12 ||
The power (śakti) is the triad of will and the rest in its collective totality; it is the tranquil state of this [consciousness] when it assumes a contracted form,
consisting of the combined nature of will and the other [powers].
But she, being real, consists of the equilibrium of the qualities beginning with sattva. || 13 ||
Prakṛti is considered to consist of the mind whose nature is the equilibrium of intellect and the other faculties;
its will is of the nature of *rajas*.
There was a sound of "haṃ," which produced the cognition of "I. || 14 ||

Its power, called Śāntā (the Quiescent), is a collective totality because it is undisturbed and because it internalizes the powers such as Will (icchā) and the rest; furthermore, due to its grasping of limitation, it is the state of non-differentiation of the qualities (guṇas), which is the principle of Prakṛti.

The triad [of the intellect, ego, and mind] arises because the qualities (guṇas) are sequentially initiated by the triad of powers beginning with will (icchā); it is from the agitation of these that the expansion of the natural creation (prākṛtika-sarga) proceeds.
Among those, within the nature of consciousness (citta), there are the intellect (buddhi), ego (ahaṃkṛt), and mind (manas).
They rest upon the state of equilibrium.

In this unfolding of the sequence of the principles (*tattva-krama-prasara*), among the classes of subjects ranging from Śiva down to the *sakala*, the powers of knowledge and action (*jñāna-śakti* and *kriyā-śakti*) alone are the primary instrument; it is these very powers that, in their contracted form, [constitute the subject].

It should be understood that *īśvara* and *śuddhavidyā* are [the levels of] contraction; *vidyā* and *kalā* are contracted; the intellect (*buddhi*) and the organs of action (*karmendriya*) are extremely contracted; and the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*) and so forth exist at the limit of the contraction of action.

The power of will (icchā-śakti) belonging to the subtle atom (aṇu), which undergoes transformation into the quality of passion (rajas), is the ego-sense (ahaṃkṛti), characterized by the conceit "I am" (ahamiti-abhimāna). || 13-14 ||
Even though it consists of *sattva*,
the intellect (*buddhi*) is the cause of determinative cognition;
its activity is composed of *tamas*.
The form is said to be the mind, which produces conceptual constructions.
The intellect (*buddhi*) is the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) itself, characterized by the determination of objects, which undergoes transformation through *sattva*;
the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) is that which undergoes transformation through *tamas*.
The principle of the mind (*manas-tattva*) is said to be characterized by the instrument of conceptualization (*vikalpa*). || 15 ||
That very same God, whose form is contracted, possesses five divisions beginning with Vāma;
he is colored by knowledge and action.
Due to its predominance, it took on the form of various objects. || 16 ||
(p. 11) That very [Lord], whose true nature consists of play and so forth, having become contracted by virtue of possessing the five forms beginning with Vāmadeva,

assumes the state of being the body of the organs of knowledge and their objects through the predominance of the coloring of the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), and [assumes] the state of the body of the organs of action through the predominance of the limiting adjunct of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*).
And it assumes the state of possessing the activity of the organs of action.
From the assumption of the five powers, the fivefold nature of the instruments (karaṇas) is to be understood. || 16 ||
The ear, eye, sense of touch, tongue, and nose are the instruments of cognition;
[their objects are] sound, touch, and form.
And taste and smell—these are the subtle elements (bhūta-sūkṣma). || 17 ||
The ears and so forth are the organs of cognition; sound and so forth are the subtle elements (tanmātras). || 17 ||
Even though he was born as the most lowly of beings, he became the Lord of Beings (Bhūteśa) through his true self;
[so too did] space, wind, and fire.
Water and earth are the five elements. || 18 ||
By assuming extreme contraction, it manifests as the five elements, beginning with space, which are insentient in nature. || 18 ||
Sound and the other [objects] are to be known by the instruments such as the ear; those [instruments] are the knowers of others.
Speech was the instrument of speaking.
The hand may be the instrument in the act of grasping.
The instruments of hearing and so forth are the means for the cognition of sound and other objects;
the organs of action, such as speech and so forth, are the means for the activities of speaking and so forth. || 19 ||
In the triad of going, emission, and bliss, the instruments are the feet and so forth;
the earth is that which possesses fragrance.
Water is characterized by natural fluidity; fire is heat.
Wind consists of the sensation of heat or the sensation of formlessness; space consists of sound;
[the body] is composed of the thirty-six principles.
I salute Śambhu, who belongs to the Kaula tradition and transcends the Kula. || 21 ||
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the anus and the generative organ are included.
Possessing odor is the defining characteristic of earth; natural fluidity is the defining characteristic of water;
fire is characterized by hot touch; air is characterized by intangible touch; and sound [is the characteristic of ether].
"Of space" refers to the designation of each primary quality individually.

Regarding the principles (tattvas), they exist in a relationship of the pervaded and the pervader in successive order; earth is the pervaded, while the thirty-five principles beginning with water and ending with Śiva are the pervaders. Thus it is in the creation of the elements.
On the earth, qualities such as space and the rest are present as pervasive accompaniments;
because the reality of Paramaśiva is omnipresent, it is precisely the nature of the Yamalakaula— both immanent in the universe and transcendent of it— that belongs to the devotees.
It has been introduced by the concluding statement of the salutation, "worthy of immersion"; may there be auspiciousness!
Thus ends the *Ṣaṭtriṃśattattvasaṃdoha*, together with the commentary composed by the venerable Rājānakānandācārya.
When the assembly of texts and learned scholars— the refuge of the six sciences— had undergone decline due to the course of time,
[the author], whose sole intent was to uphold those various true dharmas...
By one endowed with the vigor of right discernment, for the sake of the performance of action. || 1 ||
Having deliberated with his principal ministers who were devoted to righteousness, the illustrious sovereign of Kaśmīra established [this work],
which is pregnant with spiritual knowledge and worldly wisdom.
That which is the primary office for the extraction of texts. || 2 ||
May this work, having been refined by the virtuous who entered upon the livelihood [of service] under Mukunda Rāma as their presiding overseer,
stand complete through its fulfillment, purity, and exposition.
This completed work is for the welfare of virtuous people. || 3 ||
The Tilaka.
May it be offered unto the auspicious Śiva.
